newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Mar 25.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Mar 25.

text.p: Police have uncovered a huge cannabis plantation laid out like a small town and patrolled by guards with semi-automatic weapons in a remote area of the Whanganui National Park. Twelve men have been arrested after 120 police, many heavily armed, broke the biggest, most sophisticated and most remote drug operation ever found in New Zealand, Assistant Commissioner Colin Wilson said on Monday. Page 1.

New Zealand could not afford a mandatory order by the Waitangi Tribunal to return Northland state forests to Maori tribes, Treasurer Winston Peters said on Monday. It would have "serious" flow-on effects on other settlements already made, he said. "Such a settlement, if spread over other settlements on a pro-rata basis, would bankrupt the country." Page 1.

The government began a fight at the highest international trade level on Monday, against the European Union over the unique New Zealand product, spreadable butter. International Trade Minister Lockwood Smith said New Zealand had asked the

World Trade Organisation to begin a dispute resolution process in the row with the union, which began last year. The union insists on charging extra duty for the product, which it claims is not butter. Page 2.

Select committees should not be afraid to call in ministers to explain policy as part of making the government accountable, National MP Tony Ryall says. Ryall chairs the finance and expenditure select committee, which he described as the "pre-eminent" select committee. As well as scrutinising Treasury, Reserve Bank and government financial reports, it
coordinates other select committees' reviews of government departments' performances. Page 2.

A directive by Te Mangai Paho to Aotearoa Television Network to remove its first financial adviser drove them into the arms of Derek Burns, ATN director Tawini Rangihau said on Monday. She said ATN accepted Burns after he had been introduced by former and NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan and Morehu McDonald. "We thought here was a person we would trust to direct our finances. It's only now we are finding out how big a mess there is to clean up," she said. Page 2.

The Manufacturers Federation and the Employers Federation do not appear to see eye to eye over what are core issues for business, with the employers declining to support criticism of an extra $1 billion in government spending. The Employers Federation had been expected to join three other top business organisations and put its name to a critical analysis questioning the benefits of $1 billion of extra social spending, but it did not. Its deputy chief executive, Anne Knowles, said the analysis was not part of the policies and core business of employers. Page 14.

Brierley Investments is not looking to sell its 50 percent stake in giant fishing company Sealord, according to Sealord chairman Sir Tipene O'Regan. New Zealand's biggest fishing company, Sealord, is a joint venture between BIL and the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Commission. In Nelson on Monday O'Regan told a dedication function for Sealord's new $28 million factory fillet trawler, Rehua, that the rumour was doing the rounds of the waterfront. Page 14.

State-owned Landcorp has paid the government a $4 million dividend, despite making an operating loss of $1.7 million in the half-year to December 31. The loss in the latest six months was significantly smaller than the previous half-year loss of $4.8 million. Profit on the sale of land and property revaluations lifted the bottom-line return to $4.1 million in the last half-year. Page 14.

Economists forecast that data to be published on Thursday will show the New Zealand economy grew 0.4 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, giving a 17th straight quarter of growth. The range of forecasts for December quarter gross domestic production data is 0.3 percent to 0.7 percent, for a median of 0.4 percent, a survey by MMS Pacific says. Page 14.

A capital restructuring and partial float of the Port of Napier will be considered by Hawke's Bay Regional Council this week. The council, which owns 92 percent of the port, is due to decide tomorrow whether to adopt a $15 million capital restructuring recommended by the port company. It would receive a $13.8 million special dividend under the plan with the remainder going to the port's minority shareholder, Manawatu-Wanganui Regional Council. Page 14.

A group of Defiance Food Industries preference shareholders has engaged a merchant bank to try and get a cash offer of $3 a share after the company's $48 million sale to Goodman Fielder. Defiance closed on the Stock Exchange on Monday up five cents at $2.20. Merchant banker Grant Samuel and Associates believes $3 represents a fair value, and it matches the original investment made by the preference shareholders. Page 14.
